tiers.name: Manufactured mock
tiers.what: A tube mixed by a vendor from known organisms in known amounts.
tiers.truth: Vendor datasheet (strong, but DNA share is not the same as cell share).
tiers.used: ZymoBIOMICS D6300 even and D6310 log (Phase 1).
tiers.shows: Whether a tool names the right organisms and roughly the right amounts in a clean, bacteria-rich mix.
tiers.cannot: Behaviour in a mostly-human sample, rare organisms, or anything the vendor did not put in the tube.

tiers.name: Constructed from real reads
tiers.what: Real human reads with real reads of known isolates added at chosen fractions. The mix is artificial but every read is real.
tiers.truth: By construction: we know exactly how many read pairs of each organism were added.
tiers.used: Phase 2 spike-in panels: 10 organisms at 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4 and 1e-5 of 4 million read pairs, plus a human-only control.
tiers.shows: The detection limit of each tool in a blood-like, host-dominated sample, and how many false species appear with no microbe present.
tiers.cannot: Real contamination from kits, real fragment lengths of cell-free DNA, or real disease biology. The added reads come from clean isolates, so this is easier than a true low-biomass sample.

tiers.name: Real clinical, orthogonally confirmed
tiers.what: Patient samples where culture or PCR independently says which pathogen is present.
tiers.used: Not yet. The best public candidate (Uganda sepsis plasma, PRJNA898830) used a qPCR panel, but the per-sample results are not in the open supplement.
tiers.shows: Real-world accuracy, the thing that matters.
tiers.cannot: Nothing, if it existed. It is the main data gap.

tiers.name: Real, no truth
tiers.what: Real samples with no independent answer.
tiers.truth: None. We can only ask whether tools agree, whether the output looks like background contamination, and whether it is consistent with the study's description.
tiers.shows: Behaviour on real patient data: how much is human, how many species appear, how much looks like reagent contamination, whether two tools agree.
tiers.cannot: Accuracy. Agreement between tools is not correctness.

decisions.title: Every number carries a truth tier
decisions.choice: Label each result T1 to T4 (see the tiers table).
decisions.why: A species list from a manufactured mock and one from a patient sample are different kinds of evidence. Mixing them hides that.

decisions.title: The Human Microbiome Project mock was not scored
decisions.choice: Skipped it although the reads are public (SRR172902 even, SRR172903 staggered, single-end Illumina GA II).
decisions.why: I could not verify its composition from a primary source: the vendor sheets are gone (users report the product is discontinued) and the ENA record says only 'HMP Mock Community'. Remembered percentages would have been a guess presented as truth.
decisions.cost: No independent lab, no archaeon, no Streptococcus-heavy mix. Listed under 'more data'.

decisions.title: Uganda plasma data used for behaviour, not accuracy
decisions.choice: Classified 16 of 263 public runs and reported what the tools do, not whether they are right.
decisions.why: The study (PRJNA898830, 254 sepsis plasma samples plus controls) compared against a 43-pathogen qPCR panel, but the open supplement has only a workflow figure and no per-sample results, and the controls cannot be told apart in the ENA records. The reads are RNA-seq with human rRNA depleted, not DNA.
decisions.cost: Honest but weak: this tier cannot say who is right.

decisions.title: Constructed truth by spike-in
decisions.choice: Real human whole-genome reads (NA12878, 4 million pairs) plus real isolate reads at four fixed fractions; four panels rotate ten organisms so each organism meets each level once; one human-only control.
decisions.why: It is the only way to get exact truth with real reads in a host-dominated sample, and it answers the untested rare-organism question from Phase 1.
decisions.cost: Isolate reads are clean and evenly covered, human reads are DNA from a cell line, and there is no kit contamination, so detection limits here are optimistic.

decisions.title: Absolute read counts, not percentages
decisions.choice: Call a species when at least 1, 3 or 10 read pairs support it.
decisions.why: In a sample that is more than 99% human, a percentage of the profile is meaningless; what matters is how many reads a clinician could point to.
decisions.cost: Thresholds depend on sequencing depth: 10 reads at 4 million pairs is not 10 reads at 40 million.

decisions.title: Kraken2 16 GB and MetaPhlAn only
decisions.choice: Dropped the 8 GB index and Bracken for Phase 2.
decisions.why: Phase 1 showed the 8 GB index left far more reads unclassified, and Bracken estimates abundance, which is not the question for detection.

decisions.title: Reagent-contaminant genera taken from a primary source
decisions.choice: Used Table 1 of Salter et al. 2014 (BMC Biology), genera found in sequenced blank controls, as a flag.
decisions.why: Species that appear in nearly every low-biomass run are often reagent contamination, not infection.
decisions.cost: Pseudomonas, Escherichia, Bacillus and Streptococcus are on the list but can also be true pathogens, so the flag is a prompt to check a blank, not a verdict.

innovation.idea: A detection-limit curve as a standard part of every report
innovation.why: A tool that cannot see 40 reads in 4 million should say so before anyone reads its silence as absence.
innovation.first_step: Offer a mockcheck command that builds spike-ins from a user's own host and isolate reads and reports detection by fraction.

innovation.why: Compare each call against a negative control run through the same pipeline and the published contaminant genera, and mark what is probably background.
innovation.first_step: Already prototyped as a flag in the report; next is subtracting a user's own blank.

innovation.idea: Honest resolution: report the genus when the species is not supported
innovation.why: Reads that stop at genus level are the tool being right about what it knows. A forced species name is a wrong answer that looks confident.
innovation.first_step: Add a genus-fallback line to the report when most genus reads are not at species.

innovation.idea: Name the groups a tool cannot separate
innovation.why: E. coli and Shigella, or the Bacillus cereus group, look the same to short-read k-mer methods. Say so instead of picking one.
innovation.first_step: Extend config/organisms.tsv with an 'indistinguishable group' column and print it in reports.

innovation.idea: Use agreement between independent methods as a confidence signal
innovation.why: A call from a k-mer method and a marker-gene method is stronger than either alone, but this must be tested: agreement is not correctness.
innovation.first_step: Measure, on the spike-ins, whether two-tool agreement lowers the false-positive rate.

innovation.idea: Check that reads are spread across the genome
innovation.why: A species supported by reads from one conserved gene is weaker than one with even coverage.
innovation.first_step: Map reads for each called species and score evenness. Needs alignment, so heavier than Kraken2.

innovation.idea: Calibrate read thresholds to host fraction and depth
innovation.why: The right minimum read count depends on how much of the sample is human.
innovation.first_step: Fit a threshold curve from the spike-in panels and test it on the plasma runs.

innovation.why: Rank tool, database and threshold by tier, so a method strong on a clean mock but weak in a host-dominated sample cannot hide.
innovation.first_step: Publish the result tables with tier labels and a one-command submission.

needs_data.need: Clinical samples with per-sample confirmed pathogens
needs_data.why: Only real samples with culture or PCR truth test accuracy where it matters. The best public cohort found does not release per-sample reference results.
needs_data.who: Study authors, a data-sharing request, or a controlled-access dataset.

needs_data.need: Deposited negative controls and blanks, labelled
needs_data.why: Without blanks nobody can separate infection from reagent contamination.
needs_data.who: Any lab that deposits low-biomass data.

needs_data.need: More independent mocks with verifiable composition
needs_data.why: Phase 1 uses one lab and one vendor. The Human Microbiome Project mock would add an archaeon and a Streptococcus-heavy mix but its composition sheet could not be found.
needs_data.who: Vendors and archives that keep datasheets.

needs_data.why: Every run so far is a single replicate, so differences between tools have no error bars.
needs_data.who: More sequencing runs or splitting the same reads into repeated subsamples (cheap, and a good next step).

needs_data.need: Cell-free DNA fragment lengths and real library biases
needs_data.why: Spike-ins use whole-genome reads; real plasma cfDNA is short and differently biased.
needs_data.who: Public cfDNA runs from healthy donors for background, plus matching spike-in material.

needs_data.need: Viruses, parasites and more fungi with known truth
needs_data.why: The mocks contain two yeasts and no viruses, and the standard Kraken2 index has no fungi.
needs_data.who: Vendors of viral and fungal standards.

needs_data.why: Different error profile and much better species resolution; the comparison is missing.
needs_data.who: Public long-read runs of the same standards.

needs_data.why: Phase 1 found the database matters more than the algorithm; one date per database is not enough to say how much.
needs_data.who: Time and disk: a cluster job.

representation.intro: Each kind of data is stored as a small plain-text table so anyone can open it, and each table answers one question. The dictionary below is read live from the committed files.
principles: One row means one thing. The dictionary says what.
Percentages of a profile for clean mocks (T1), absolute read pairs for host-dominated samples (T2, T4).
Truth is a separate table from observations, never mixed into the tool output.
Every table is small enough to commit. Raw classifier reports are kept in results/raw so every number can be recomputed with one command.
Strict and relaxed scoring sit side by side, with the relaxed columns labelled.
